channel.title: From the Cabinet
channel.description: A living cabinet of essays, dialogues, and slow notes on philosophy, theology, and attention.

item.title: Timon, on authenticity.
item.description: What if you could take the journey of your dreams, see everything you ever wanted to see, and experience it all exactly as you wished but no one could ever know you had been there? Would the journey still be worth the same?
item.content:encoded:
AlexanderGreetings, Timon! I saw your prints yesterday… on the wall. It seems the land of the Thais is a veritable paradise. Matthew even mentioned to me that everyone in the city has already heard about your adventures.

TimonOh yes, Alexander! Traveling is my greatest passion. I’ve been to half the world already. Nothing broadens one’s horizons or enriches a person quite like it. You should try it sometime instead of merely reading all those books of yours.

AlexanderPerhaps you are right, my friend. But tell me, as a distinguished expert on the subject: what exactly does this passion consist in?

TimonIt’s simple. It means discovering new cultures, tasting local foods, having adventures for yourself. It is pure experience of the world and the making of memories that stay with you forever.

AlexanderIt sounds noble indeed. Then the essence of traveling is the personal experience itself, which takes place within you, Timon?

TimonPrecisely. You change as a person. Wouldn’t you agree, Matthew?

MatthewBy the gods, Timon, I rather think I've been the same man for years! Though perhaps that's only how it seems to us.

AlexanderThen, if I understand you correctly, the value of a journey exists independently of whether anyone ever learns of it?

TimonOf course.

AlexanderEven if no one ever saw your pictures?

TimonEven then.

AlexanderEven if you could not tell a single person about it?

TimonYes. Surely the memories would still be mine.

AlexanderInteresting. And yet I have heard that ever since you returned, you have done little but tell people about your latest adventures. It makes me wonder… if you had lost your voice and brought back no pictures from there, would your journey have been just as successful?

TimonWell, I would have been terribly sorry to lose the keepsakes, but of course it would have, Alexander. I would still have the experiences and the images in my head.

AlexanderI understand. Let us imagine, then, Timon, a somewhat different situation.

Imagine that some evil seer, or perhaps some god, casts a curse upon you. You may go wherever on Earth you please, Timon, stay in the finest hotels, watch the most beautiful sunsets over the ocean. You may even meet people you have always wanted to meet.

But there is one condition: absolutely no one may ever find out about it.

TimonWhat do you mean?

AlexanderYou may not keep a single picture, nor send anyone so much as a thought about the journey. You may not even mention the journey, not a word, to any of your friends for the rest of your life. You return from the land of the Thais and must pretend that you spent the entire month sitting in your little apartment.

TimonThat is a very peculiar premise, Alexander.

AlexanderBut answer me, please. If the essence of passion is, as you yourself said a moment ago, “pure experience of the world and the making of memories,” then not being able to tell others about it should not make the journey itself any less valuable. So would you set out on such a wonderful journey just as eagerly, and with the very same enthusiasm?

TimonTo tell you the truth… I find it rather difficult to answer that so neatly now.

AlexanderWhy?

TimonI would feel some kind of emptiness. As though the whole thing were happening only halfway.

AlexanderBut you would still see the ocean.

TimonI know.

AlexanderYou would still eat the local food.

TimonHow could I not?

AlexanderYou would still have the memories.

TimonThat is true.

AlexanderAnd yet something would be missing?

TimonYes.

AlexanderWhat, Timon? You would have your dream journey, all to yourself.

TimonI don’t know. Perhaps the awareness that other people know I was there.

AlexanderThen the gaze of others turns out to be part of your experience?

TimonI suppose so.

AlexanderThen it is no longer entirely “pure”?

TimonI don’t know, Alexander. The way you keep putting all this to me, I can hardly tell anymore what I myself thought about it a moment ago.

AlexanderThen do you truly love traveling, or do you rather love the fact that other people see you traveling?

TimonYou’re beginning to annoy me, Alexander. Are you suggesting that I spend a fortune on holidays merely for recognition and applause?

AlexanderI am suggesting nothing. I am merely trying to follow your own logic.

TimonBut that is hardly fair. The fact that I like other people to see my travels does not mean that I do not like the travels themselves.

AlexanderSo you claim that you can want two things at once?

TimonOf course.

AlexanderTo travel for yourself and, at the same time, to travel for others?

TimonYes.

AlexanderThen your first definition was incomplete.

TimonPerhaps.

AlexanderAnd if it was incomplete, can we still say that you know the essence of your passion?

TimonI don’t know, Alexander. You’re clearly driving at something, and you keep twisting my words until I’m completely confused.

AlexanderAnd so once again, we know nothing.

TimonPerhaps you know nothing. I know at least that I like the land of the Thais.

AlexanderThat is something to begin with.

---

AlexanderLet us look more broadly, Timon, at other pursuits. Perhaps that will bring us closer to what we are looking for.

You certainly know people who have taken up extreme running, climbed mountains at dawn, or begun baking artisan sourdough bread at home?

TimonI know many. I myself started baking bread last year.

AlexanderAnd I suppose pictures of those beautiful, crusty loaves immediately made their way out into the city as well?

TimonWell, yes… Sometimes decorating the cuts in the dough took me longer than kneading it. I was immensely proud of them!

AlexanderAnd if you were unable to show them off?

TimonThe bread would still taste good.

AlexanderBut would you bake it with the same enthusiasm?

TimonI don’t know that, Alexander, but I would have to feed myself somehow anyway.

AlexanderThen let us consider, dear Timon: if everyone around us were to stop listening to our boasts tomorrow, once and for all; if every way of announcing our triumphs to the world were suddenly to disappear… how many of these “enthusiasts” would rather sleep two hours longer in the morning than run through mud in the freezing cold?

How many devoted travelers, instead of rattling around by airplane to some exotic, humid jungle full of mosquitoes, would rather go to the nearby lake simply to rest?

TimonBy the gods, Alexander, it is hard to pass judgment on such a thing, but perhaps most of them.

AlexanderHow so?

TimonSometimes I go to an exhibition opening not to look at the paintings, but to mark my presence in a place of culture.

AlexanderThen, my dear Timon, must we not arrive at the sad conclusion that for many of us passions are not at all a search for an activity, but a search for an audience? Travel is no longer an end in itself, but merely expensive scenery for a spectacle in which we play the leading role before the crowd?

TimonHeavens above, Alexander… I think you’ve driven me into a corner. If the audience disappeared, the theaters of our magnificent passions would be empty in a single day.

AlexanderAnd you, Matthew? What is your view of this whole matter?

MatthewSince I have finally been noticed. There is something peculiar about all this.

AlexanderWhat is that?

MatthewThat you moved so quickly from asking questions to passing judgment.

AlexanderHave I not demonstrated that Timon is dependent upon the audience?

MatthewYou demonstrated that he cares about the audience. That is not necessarily the same thing.

AlexanderWell said, Matthew. But tell me, then, where exactly are we going wrong here?

MatthewI do not yet know whether we are wrong, but we are certainly hasty.

AlexanderIn what way was I hasty?

MatthewIn assuming that a man cares only about what others think of him. For how do the thoughts of others about us diminish our actions, so that what we do thereby becomes less genuine? Does one thing really follow from the other?

AlexanderIf someone bakes bread more for praise than for the bread itself, then surely there is something to it, my friend!

MatthewBut did you say that he bakes it more for praise?

AlexanderHe himself admitted that he did not know whether he would do it with the same enthusiasm if no one could praise him.

MatthewHe did not say that he would stop baking altogether.

TimonBy the gods, my friends, I don’t know, but somehow it seems to me that I would not stop entirely. Perhaps I would bake less often and would not attach quite so much importance to it.

AlexanderAnd that is precisely what I am talking about.

MatthewAbout what?

AlexanderAbout the public influencing what we do. Not merely whether we do something. If you bake bread differently because you know you will later show it to others, then you are no longer baking it entirely for yourself.

MatthewThere is some truth in that. But do not congratulate yourself just yet, Alexander. I want to ask you something else first. Is it always bad for the gaze of others to influence what we do?

AlexanderWell, surely not always.

MatthewIndeed, it is hard to cut oneself off completely from other people’s eyes and opinions.

AlexanderImpossible.

MatthewUnless you intend to go and live in the forest.

TimonAnd then you would probably start worrying about what the wolves think of you.

AlexanderVery funny.

MatthewBut precisely because we live among others, is it not a good and proper thing that we wish to be well regarded by them?

AlexanderNaturally, Matthew. But natural does not mean good.

MatthewPerhaps so. But does it mean, by definition, that it is bad?

AlexanderNo.

MatthewThen you yourself already distinguish between two things.

AlexanderWhat things?

MatthewThe fact that we want to be well regarded, and the fact that we subordinate all our actions to that desire.

AlexanderPerhaps.

MatthewTell me, then: when you dress neatly in the morning, do you do so partly because you will meet other people?

AlexanderOf course.

MatthewAnd if you knew you would be alone all day, would you dress differently?

AlexanderProbably.

MatthewAnd does that mean you are pretending?

AlexanderNo.

MatthewAre you creating some image of yourself?

AlexanderYes, certainly.

MatthewAnd you see nothing wrong with that?

AlexanderNot really, by the gods. I scarcely think about it at all!

MatthewYou do it for others, but also partly for yourself, because you like the way you look? So a little for yourself, a little for others?

AlexanderEven then I see nothing wrong with it.

MatthewAnd what if it were ninety percent for others?

AlexanderThen I would begin to wonder.

MatthewAnd what if it were ninety-nine?

AlexanderThen I suppose I really would no longer be dressing for myself.

MatthewThen perhaps the problem is not the gaze of others itself, but its priority in our actions.

AlexanderThat may well be so.

TimonSo if I stop asking, “Do I like this?” and begin asking “Does everyone else approve of it?” only then something changes.

AlexanderBut that still does not prove that the public is something particularly bad.

MatthewI did not say it was.

AlexanderThen how would you put it into words, Matthew, and make your case to us? For it is already becoming quite clear that there is something to all this.

MatthewAs we sit here talking, we look at one another, and something rather natural becomes clear: whenever we speak to one another, we are also watching one another.

AlexanderOf course.

MatthewAnd does that influence your behavior?

AlexanderHow could it not?

MatthewAnd how many people are looking at you right now?

AlexanderYou, Matthew, and Timon -that would give us two pairs of eyes!

MatthewAnd if a hundred were watching you, how would you behave?

AlexanderProbably somewhat differently.

MatthewAnd if a thousand?

AlexanderDifferently again.

MatthewAnd if a hundred thousand?

AlexanderI don’t know, by the gods, Matthew. I have never seen so many people in my life!

MatthewBut can you imagine that the difference would be small?

AlexanderNo.

MatthewBecause the more people are watching, the more a person begins to think about it, grows anxious, and is eaten alive by stage fright. Is that not so? And what if they were not all watching at once, but could be watching at any moment?

AlexanderThat would be even worse!

TimonAnd is that how our city works?

MatthewNo. In the city you can, after all, walk away from people. Here, anyone can be an audience, even someone you have never met. The problem is no longer merely that we show ourselves to others. It is that we may begin to live as though we were being watched all the time.

AlexanderThat really does change things.

MatthewBut does all of this mean that whatever we show becomes false?

AlexanderNo.

MatthewIs every keepsake from a beautiful journey a lie?

AlexanderNo.

MatthewIs every act of boasting about a success hypocrisy?

AlexanderNo.

MatthewThen can we preserve our first insight?

AlexanderWhich one?

MatthewThat the audience may influence our actions without necessairly making those actions automatically false.

AlexanderThat is how it seems to us now.

MatthewAnd that sometimes it is good to keep something hidden?

AlexanderAbsolutely. Not everything that is true needs to be shown.

TimonThat, at least, sounds like a relief.

MatthewWhy?

TimonBecause I was beginning to think that if I wanted to be honest, then starting tomorrow I ought to record not only every beautiful sunset, but also every argument, every failure, and every day when I sit at home and cannot be bothered to do anything.

AlexanderNow that would be a peculiar performance!

MatthewSo we agree that privacy is not hypocrisy?

AlexanderYes.

MatthewAnd that showing oneself is not, in itself, hypocrisy?

AlexanderYes.

MatthewBut that the desire to show oneself can sometimes change what we do?

AlexanderYes.

MatthewAnd even what we begin to desire?

AlexanderI think that is precisely the worst of it. And now it seems to me, dear Matthew, that this is what I was looking for all along, and what I was really trying to show Timon when we began speaking earlier.

TimonHow so?

AlexanderBecause if I begin choosing a journey not because I want to go somewhere, but because I want to have something to show, then the public is no longer merely a witness to the journey. It becomes one of the reasons for taking it in the first place, and one of the reasons it takes the form it does.

MatthewSo you would no longer say that the journey is false because of that?

AlexanderI would rather say that it becomes partly someone else’s. If I go somewhere in order to experience something for myself, but at the same time choose the place, the clothes, the food, and even the angle from which I look at something while thinking only about how it will appear to others, then part of my choice no longer belongs to me alone.

MatthewThat is a stronger claim.

AlexanderBut I think it is a more honest one than the claim with which I began.

MatthewHow so?

AlexanderBecause earlier I wanted to say: “If you need an audience, then your passion is false.” Now I would rather say: “If the audience begins deciding what you desire, then you ought to be careful.”

TimonSo you have not refuted me after all, Alexander.

AlexanderThat was not my intention; though Matthew has been of great help to us here.

MatthewHelp with what?

AlexanderWith making sure I do not say more than what truly follows from what we have discovered anew here.

item.title: The Phenomenology and Certainty
item.description: Science produces precise but constrained abstractions of experience, while metaphysics investigates the conditions that make experience possible; both contribute to understanding, but only within a cycle that returns them to the Life-World.
item.content:encoded:
There’s a common mistake that shows up constantly in a modern discourse - we treat scientific knowledge as if it floats above experience. Many assume it even replaces the experience rather than emerges from it. The diagram below is meant to challenge that assumption - not by rejecting the science itself, but by placing it more precisely within a broader pipeline of quest for certainty.

At the foundation lies what phenomenologists call the Life-World - a raw, lived experience. This is the world as it is given - before theories, measurements or any interpretations. It’s messy but it’s also the only place anything ever actually shows up.

From there we perform phenomenological reduction. It's an attempt to suspend assumptions. But here's a shocker - interpretation doesn’t begin with science. It begins with commitment.

Before we do science or metaphysics, we specifically choose how we’re going to interpret reality. Science isn't born from nothing. It's built on a foundation to treat reality in a particular, constrained way. Science constantly narrows its focus. It strips away subjective, qualitative aspects of experience and replaces them with measurable, formalized structures.

Both paths (mataphysics and naturalism) merge into a local synthesis. This is a contextual integration of formal knowledge (from science) and lived meaning (from experience and metaphysical analysis). This synthesis is local because it depends on context, purpose, and domain. There is no single, final perspective.

So which perspective takes priority? Well, it depends on the context really. What is important is that metaphysics and science are not interchangeble. Naturalistic models can reshape our experience interpretations, but they cannot invalidate the fact of that experience itself.

item.title: The Wall and Nausea
item.description: Being truly conscious means existing in a painful superposition between a social system and the honest, dull silence of the 'In-Itself' and reality.
item.content:encoded:
There is a peculiar kind of exhaustion that really does not come from simply doing too much. And it doesn’t really come from doing too little. It comes from seeing too clearly.

Sartre called it la nausée and it is the main motive of his novel - Nausea1. Roquentin (which is the main guy in the book) first experiences it when he picks up a pebble on a beach, and suddenly, he cannot put it down for some reason. Not because the pebble is special, but rather because it is not. Because it just is, positioned between his fingers, unnecessarily there, indifferent to being held. It is only then when Roquentin realizes that pebble, and for all it matters the whole world, does not need to be here; neither does he himself. There is nothing grand behind that existence, no plan, no architecture, no mission - all there is is for no reason whatsoever.

And in that moment the greatest ones that depicted that dread, bring up instant remedies. Camus says: go swim, eat something good, go for a walk and consume the sun, coffee and conversations - instead of analyzing and dissecting existence, start to feel it. Sartre says: commit to a project3, author yourself, fill the nothingness with action. To me, both of them essentially say: look away.

Both cures are in a sense forms of the Sunday parade - that scene in Nausea where the citizens of Bouville tip their hats to each other, walk their routes, and perform their purposes. The hikers hiking. The marathoners running. The people on their missions tunnelling their field of view until that void, that nothingness, the hollow everyday life is out of their scope.

What then remains beyond is simply sitting and staring at the wall. At least it looks honest. Not productive, not comfortable, not special - but honest. It does not pretend it leads anywhere. The Sunday crowd creates fake edifice, the wall-starer just sits there and admits there is nothing to it. The wall-starer is definitely not winning in “the game of life” - but they have stopped losing.23

Yet there is one main issue in that logic - you can't just live the wall.

Not because it is fundamentally wrong, I wouldn’t say that. And not because the feeling of nausea is a mistake that must be fixed or corrected in our typical human manner.

It's because there is a system, and it doesn't care that you've seen through it. It shouts - sends emails, schedules things and organizes your life; shows you the newest trends, makes you play certain roles. Sitting still on a Wednesday afternoon suddenly is like a crime. That system has built an entire civilization around the concepts of doing something, and ideally something meaningful.

We are slaves of our own doing, but not in some poetic sense. Practically. You try to stare at the wall, and the system shouts - your mind starts evaluating your week, and suddenly you're back inside the machine you were trying to opt out of.

This is a being that is fixed between two equally unbearable poles. On one side the raw, dull weight of existence. Nausea, the wall. On the other side - the system, the Sunday parade. The demands of productivity, friendship and meaning. The distraction that masks the void, a distraction that grips your insides whether you consent or not.

To be conscious enough to see both is to be caught in the middle. And I mean caught like in a can't-fully-rest-anywhere way.

You are at work, and you are thinking of the wall; then you are at the wall, and the system is shouting about what you should be doing with your one wild adventurous life.

This is what Sartre meant when he said we are a "useless passion", we are the only beings that demand why, and the universe is the only entity that provides what.

Perhaps the only thing left in that superposition of hanging between the hammer and the anvil is to stop asking for an instant remedy. Maybe let’s start getting curious about what it actually is like to live in the middle, without any cure.

Petty life, the only one there is. Not a tragedy - just what it is.

References & Notes

  1. Which of course I strongly recommend reading
  2. One must imagine Sisyphus happy lol
  3. I reckon Sartre would say that the sole idea of "wall staring" is a projet of its own; I am not gonna argue with that.
  4. One must imagine Sysyphus happy lol

item.title: The Sartrean Trap
item.description: When the method becomes a prison - on how Sartre misused phenomenology. 'And if phenomenology refuses to step outside of itself, then isn't it becoming the very thing it was meant to battle?'
item.content:encoded:
Husserl

The beginnings of the twentieth century really entangled philosophers in a peculiar state of paralysis. Many discussions no matter how local, or global, practical or theoretical, risked being dissolved into a somewhat tragic, the same final matter of “Is the world even real? How could we know for certain? What is the relation between that real world and a human mind?”. All the legitimate, somehow inevitable questions,yet fatal to any pragmatic discussion. When every issue collapses into the foundational dilemma, none could be resolved really.

Husserl’s phenomenology was a methodological breakthrough.1 Epoche - the suspension of any assumptions (including metaphysical ones) was one of the finest inventions. Yet, Husserl did not deny the world, nor declared metaphysics obsolete, nonfactual, a fairy. He proposed a tool, a way of setting aside any prejudices, biases, dilemmas and worldviews temporarily in order to examine what is given in the experience, as it appears, and analyse the phenomenon further in that manner. The universe itself is not rejected, rather placed between (or behind) the brackets so that human consciousness, experience, meaning and appearance could be studied without distractions.

I believe Husserl’s intentions were of a pragmatic nature, very epistemology-centered. He sought clarity in that process of dissection and analyses, not an ultimate worldview or holistic picture of how things really are. One could think of it rather like metaphysics is being postponed, not abolished. Bracketing is thorough and strategic, but temporary and most importantly - limited. It is a suspension for the sake of focus, one could not conclude from this that nothing for certain lies beyond the bracket.

Husserl’s tool allows us to examine the gallery paintings without really thinking about where the gallery building is located, what are its foundations made of, and which side of the world the main entrance is facing. Most importantly, by the use of phenomenology none of us is bothered by the question whether that art gallery exists at all, yet that phenomenology itself does not claim that those questions do not matter.

What may be bothering is that many thinkers after Husserl misused that tool to create from it an ontology of its own.

Sartre

Sartre inherits Husserl's method but fundamentally transforms the scope of it. What was meant to be just a method in frenchmen’s hands becomes a complex picture of reality. Sartre’s phenomenology, especially in Being and Nothingness, presents more as an extensive ontology. He describes consciousness, the for-itself, the in-itself, freedom, nothingness, and the structure of human existence like a cartographer mapping a continent that is fully accessible with use of pure experience. So he does not use phenomenology to analyze the reality, rather speaks of his observations as they were exhausting the whole picture of what there is. A tool becomes a worldview. As Sartre says in Being and Nothingness:

"The being of an existent is precisely what it appears"

His identification of phenomenological description as ontology is precisely where the problem arises. He never recovers from the epoche and stays in the bracket, moreover his whole universe is built within it. If we were to freeze that viewpoint I would argue that this suspension, that epoche from metaphysical plain becomes a metaphysical claim itself - for Sartre what lies beyond human experience and appearance is philosophically irrelevant. In his world the universe in essence is just an insignificant background for human existence. Everything apart from his concept of for-itself (and the actions revolving around it) is really diminished to the role of in-itself - muted, grayed out, secondary, unimportant.

This results in a creation of a claustrophobic system, in which human perspective becomes the axis around which everything else - including ontology - revolves. The complexity of what lies beyond the experience is silently omitted. Not negated, not refuted, not examined - neglected and left out.

In that context, what was meant for us to help us see clearer (phenomenology) becomes a boundary of what was ever allowed to be seen.

The mistake

Husserl’s bracketing was never meant to define the limits of reality, yet Sartre treats it as if it does. He speaks of phenomenological appearances as if they were ontological structures, I would call that a category error. The method of describing experiences does not cover the totality of what there ultimately is.

However, Sartre’s viewpoint does not eliminate metaphysics, rather produces an accidental one. To rely exclusively on what appears to us is itself a leap of faith, no more no less than the leap needed to reject or affirm religious belief. This assumes that appearance, pictured by human consciousness, is sufficient enough to create and ground ontologies, a whole system to be precise. It’s an unnoticed, neglected but very real metaphysical commitment.

Here, I would argue, works of Kant and Husserl are often misinterpreted or not understood fully. Neither of them claimed to have resolved the structure and outlines of reality; Kant limited knowledge to phenomena, yet insisted on existence of the noumenal. Husserl limited scope of analysis to appearance, but for the sake of clarity, not as a way to claim that appearance is the totality. Sartre acts as if those limits were the edge of the knowledgeable world (or rather what edge of what there is meaningful in it).

This of course leads to human-centered ontology, where human is not only the only essence of meaning but really the only lens through which meaning is really seen and existent. The rest - what lies beyond the field of view of that lens - is just a noise. So one cannot say Sartre disposes of that part of reality, there is something besides what there is to be viewed through the lens - he just leaves it unaddressed.

The call

What is needed is not rejection of phenomenology, but a proper use of it. Husserl’s work remains invaluable. It allows focused inquiry and protects philosophy from endless doubts and debates that quake the ground of every new discussion. However, phenomenology must remain what it was intended to be - a tool, with all its limits, flaws and burdens.

We need philosophies that can use that tool without being enclosed by it, philosophies that examine experience but still remain open for what there is beyond, philosophies that postpone metaphysics but do not settle on that.

Phenomenology should assist us in seeing further, not limit us on what we are allowed to see. It is a starting point of an analysis, not its final boundary. And to be faithful to its task, after it is being used, the epoche must be set aside.

Husserl gave us a discipline of thought, Sartre turned it into a universe. The task now is to restore the original proportion.
And if phenomenology refuses to step outside of itself, then isn't it becoming the very thing it was meant to battle?

References & Notes

  1. E. Husserl developed phenomenology, a philosophical method in the early 1900s. I recommend reading his The Crisis of European Sciences and Transcendental Phenomenology, especially §10 to §15, before reading that article :)

item.title: Christocentric Determinism
item.description: On bridging the theological tension between arminianism and calvinism. Creating a doctrine that might be both true to the gospel and intellectually satisfying.
item.content:encoded:
The history of christian dogmatics is characterized by a persistent dialectical tension between divine sovereignty and human responsibility. Traditional resolutions (specifically calvinism and arminianism) inevitably compromise one divine attribute to preserve another: the former sacrificing universal benevolence whereas the latter is sacrificing omnipotence and absolute’s allpowerfulness. This text proposes a distinct theological architecture - sovereign universal election with selective activation. This system presupposes that the objective status of election is universal (via the incarnation) while the subjective actualization of that status is strictly determined by a sovereign, efficient divinity. This framework acts as a bridge between the absolute determinism required by a coherent idea of absolute’s essence and the mandates and ideas of salvation found within the gospel.

The unconditioned absolute

To construct a robust theology of election, one must first establish a metaphysics of the divine nature that does not collapse under thorough observations. If God is defined as the infinite, eternal, unconditioned substance, then the existence of an autonomous human will that is capable of roaming freely as it wills independently of that God is a logical impossibility.

As Baruch Spinoza states in his Ethics, a substance that is infinite cannot be limited by anything external to itself. If the human will were a "kingdom within a kingdom" capable of resisting the divine will then God would cease to be the unconditioned and all-powerful - and thus would be reduced to a powerfull but not all-powerfull being in the universe. However, that universe must be understood not as a cloud of independent possibilities, but as a closed, preplanned framing that had been once ruled by the absolute. Every thought, idea, and action that is present within the order of that universe must be a mode of the singular divine substance.

In this deterministic framework a man is just a node that resides in the logic of the universe. One is governed to endure being and that being is entirely determined by causes which ultimately trace back to the sovereign decree of God.

Breaking the calvinist limits

Where strict spinozism leads to an impersonal nature of human life, christian theology introduces the Logos - a person of Jesus. However, unlike the calvinist reformed viewpoint which limits Jesus’ intervention to a pre selected few (limited atonement) his teaching points to a rather universal scope.
In John 12:32 Jesus says:

"and I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself"

This declaration establishes the universal status of election, which seems to be an almoast legal-like statement, a reality. When Christ died he brought together the entire universe. The election must be universal as the incarnation united God with all humanity and not just a specific list of names. To argue otherwise is to limit the value of Christ’s sacrifice and his own teachings (and maybe his own divinity as well?). So basically, every human being lives under the scope of universal election.

This might be similar to some views of Karl Barth (“humanity is elected in Christ"). The doors of salvation are legally open to every single human being. God is not a tyrant who creates people for destruction as he has objectively reconciled the world with himself.

Sovereign activation - challenging the arminian boldness

If everyone is drawn, why isn’t everyone saved? While the status of the election is universal, the reality of faith is not. This discrepancy is not explained by human free will (that essentially subtracts from God's omnipotent substance) but rather the doctrine of sovereign activation.
A finite human cannot choose the infinite (unless the infinite divinity causes that choice). This is where Jesus, in John 6:65, specifies his soteriological framework further:

"This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father"

In this system, salvation occurs through sovereign activation. The lost are simply those operating on the default laws and nature of the universe, whereas the saved are those in whom God activated the divine calling. Note, that this activation could not be a cooperative effort, like a 50/50 effort split between human and the absolute.

This activation may be similar to a mechanism of efficient grace or middle knowledge. The all knowing God, perceiving the infinite timeline of cause and effect, applies irresistible grace that is consistent with one’s path of life and experiences. The difference between the believer and the non-believer is not a difference of morality, ethics or wisdom, rather a different state of sanctification caused by God's action. One has been activated by will and grace of the absolute and the other remain in the fog of default natural state.

Phenomenology of the facade of free will

If the mechanism of salvation is strictly deterministic, how does one account for the existential experience of choice and repentance?

Because we cannot see the exact contents of God’s election decree, one experiences the activation as a desperate, personal crisis; a weight of choice that essentially acts as a phenomenological facade - a free will. This facade is not a deception but act of mercy. It is a structural necessity for love, love which by its nature, requires a subject-to-subject relationship. If one were to perceive itself purely as a puppet of the divine substance the relationshp would collapse. The illusion of autonomy is a necessity in which the reality of God’s love is felt and reciprocated. It allows the finite being to engage with dynamics of the universe and personal relation with the infinite God. If we saw ourselves as mere cogs in a machine, we would despair.

In Deleuze’s terms the universal election is the virtual reality - fully present but not yet actualized on the subject. The activation is the event that breaks in the virtual into the actual, manifesting activation process as acts of faith. The facade of choice is the medium through which this actualization is experienced by human beings.

Mystery of the lost

The inevitable question arises regarding those who are never activated - the lost. Why doesn’t the absolute activate everyone?
In this system their lack of activation is not a failure of God’s power (nor an act of successful resistance against thereof). As stated before, they are those who simply were chosen to live within the logic and laws of the universe, and nothing more. Romans 11:32 emphasizes on that idea:

"for God has bound everyone over to disobedience so that he may have mercy on them all"

That obligation is a positive act of the sovereign God to maintain a portion of humanity in the natural state. This creates a state of tragic necessity: the "vessels of common use" provide the necessary contrast for the revelation of glory to the "vessels of mercy" (vide Romans 9). The non-activated are integral to the divine plan as their existence in the nature highlights the miracle of God’s grace beside it.

Whether these individuals lack a specific component or simply were not meant to be recipients of the divine call is second-degree matter. The Sovereign did not activate the action of faith within them. They remain recipients of the general election in Christ, but without the subjective activation required to transition from the logic of nature to the logic of salvation.

We are left with the certainty that they:

  1. were included in the universal election (Jesus died for them)
  2. remain in the logic of the nature by absolute’s sovereign doing
  3. their existence serves the glory of the whole by providing the contrast necessary for grace to be recognized as grace

Conclusion

The idea of sovereign universal election with selective activation offers a robust theological fortress that tends to withstand logic and complies with biblical reasoning.1 It allows God’s absolute sovereignty (Spinoza) and affirms that he is the only power, cause and only will. However, through the mystery of the incarnation, it allows him to be Jesus - merciful god that draws all humanity.
It asserts that we are fully determined and fully responsible - universally called yet selectively chosen. With no room for self-pride (arminianism) and no room for despair (calvinism) - maybe only just with the "fear and trembling" of a being held in the hands of an omnipotent, almighty divine power.

God is not a passive observer (that relies on human cooperation), nor he is an illogical tyrant limiting the love he promised to all. In the mystery of his divinity one could describe him as an architect of a deterministic world, who had been sovereignly choosing to actualize his universal love in the specific, miraculous events on individual beings. Leaving the remaining mass of the universe as a means that testify his grace and power.

I don't claim to solve the moral equations of why the absolute activates some and omits the others. I argue that to solve this mystery by diminishing God's power or lessening Christ’s reach is far greater error. I accept the silence of the lost as terrifying that prerogative might be. Maybe this is the way that preserves divine substance and its atrtributes cohesieve and intact.

References & Notes

  1. Only to some extent, a month after writing that article it came to me that maybe it's not as foolproof as it could be :) I reckon calvinism itself and supralapsarian view of absolute's doings are not as well-thought as I use to think back then.

item.title: Welcome!
item.description: Hi! Thank you for visiting my blog :)
item.content:encoded:
Thank you for visiting my website :) I will be posting notes, essays and my takes and considerations here mostly on philosophy and theology.

The Premise

This site is a home for slow reading: careful arguments, field notes, and reflective drafts. Each piece was written to be read without distraction :)

This newsletter focuses primarily on philosophy, with regular excursions into theology and metaphysics
You can expect essays that explore:

  • nature of substance: determinism, free will, and what it means for something to be real

  • theological synthesis: analyzing religious concepts through philosophical logic

  • notes & reviews: thoughts on texts, thinkers, and cultural moments

The Cadence

I value depth over frequency; I will try to publish once a month :)
However, the goal is not not to achieve maximum clarity, but rather a snapshot of thought; the slow construction of arguments that can be revisited over the years.

Who this is for?

This is for the curious. Whether you are a secular philosopher, a religious believer, or someone simply trying to read some thoughts on this machine called a universe, you are welcome here.

I leave dogmatism at the door in favor of logic, structure, and honest exploration.
